Derivation of \(P(A)\) as a Function of \(k\)

The task is to find the probability that 2 people or more people have the same birthday given a random sample size of k people. We are to assume 365 days per year and that all birthdays are equally likely. (Picture of handwritten work is at the end of this document)

I’m going to start by defining the event and any variables:

\(A:\) {2 or more people have the same birthday}

\(k =\) number of people in random sample

The way I’m going to approach this is by using the complement event to solve for the probability of interest:

\(A^c:\) {Each person has a unique birthday}

In this way we can represent \(P(A)\) as \(P(A) = 1 - P(A^c)\)

So, how many outcomes are there that represent unique birthdays among k people? This makes me think of the permutation rule that states1:

If you are drawing n elements from a set of N elements and arranging the n elements in a distinct order, the number of different results is:

\[ P_n^N = \frac{N!}{(N-n)!} \]

With this we can get the number of favorable outcomes (all k people having unique birthdays), and then in order to get \(P(A^c)\) we need to divide by the sample space which can be represented using the multiplicative rule that states1:

If you are drawing one element from each of k sets of elements, with the sizes of the sets \(n_1,n_2,n_3...,n_k\) the number of different results is:

\[ n_1n_2n_3...n_k \]

Which will be the number of total outcomes (any day being a birthday) that are possible for k people since each has 365 days of potential birthdays.

We can now represent \(P(A^c)\) as the following equation

\[ P(A^c) = \frac{P_k^{365}}{365^k} = \frac{\frac{365!}{(365-k)!}}{365^k} \]

and subsequently we can then use this to solve for \(P(A)\):

\[ P(A) = 1-P(A^c) \]

Code and Function Evaluation

Now to implement this in code as a function and evaluate at chosen values of k

# Define the function ptormore with k as the argument
ptormore <- function(k){
  
  if(k<2){ # Allow error so we know to keep k >= 2
    
    stop("Sample size (k) is less than 2. This function for the probability of 2 or more people sharing the same birthday requires k >= 2 in order to be evaluated")
    
  }
  else{
    # using minus and multiplication because dealing with logs 
    # using logs because values get too large for computation in R -- results in inf
    logperm <- (lfactorial(365) - lfactorial(365-k)) - (k*log(365))
    
    # get log permutation value back to permuation value 
    pAc <- exp(logperm) 
    
    # get pA using complementation
    pA <- 1 - pAc
    
    # return probability
    return(pA)
    
  }
}

Evaluate the function at k = 30

ptormore(30)
## [1] 0.7063162

This results in a probability of ~70.6% that 2 or more people out of 30 total people will share the same birthday given 365 days in a year and and that all birthdays are equally likely.
